column1: # The grammar pair: abnf(src) and parse(g, v) -- G9.
# Columns: name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect ; modes: gens|errc ; escapes: \n \t \\
# abnf(src) COMPILES an RFC 5234 grammar and answers the grammar
# SOURCE, so a parser is an ordinary string: it canons, it hashes and it
# unifies with no new kind in the lattice. The compile is what the call
# is for -- a grammar that does not compile is refused at the
# DECLARATION rather than at every site that parses with it.
# parse(g, v) applies the grammar and answers the tabnas AST --
# {rule, src, kids} all the way down -- as ordinary maps and lists.
# `kids` is always present and always a list, so a vocabulary written
# against the AST need not ask whether a leaf has the key.
# parse(g) -- the ONE-ARGUMENT form -- is the same grammar as a
# CONSTRAINT on whatever meets it, which is what a schema position
# wants where there is no value yet to hand the call.
# Every expectation was obtained by running BOTH engines and requiring
# agreement.
abnf-answers-the-grammar-source
parse-answers-the-ast
parse-single-leaf
parse-grammar-inline
parse-nested-rules
# A FAILURE TO PARSE IS A FAILURE TO UNIFY: the call answers a located
# nil, so the field is refused rather than set to a value meaning "no".
parse-refuses-text-outside-the-grammar
parse-refuses-a-trailing-remainder
# THE EMPTY STRING IS NOT A PARSE. Both host engines answer an empty
# tree for empty input rather than refusing it, which would make
# parse(g, "") succeed under EVERY grammar; a validator whose whole job
# is to refuse malformed input cannot have that.
parse-refuses-the-empty-string
# A grammar that does not compile is refused where it is DECLARED, with
# the compiler's own first line as the reason.
abnf-refuses-a-grammar-that-does-not-compile
abnf-refuses-an-undefined-rule
# THE CONSTRAINT FORM is VALUE-PRESERVING, like every other atom in the
# algebra: it admits the string it was written with and answers that
# string, which is what keeps it idempotent and order-independent under
# a meet. The tree is what the two-argument form is for.
parse-constraint-admits-its-peer
parse-constraint-is-order-independent
parse-constraint-is-idempotent
# THE DEFAULT SITS BESIDE IT, which is the whole reason for the form:
# `*"" | parse(G)` is either the default or a string the grammar takes.
parse-constraint-defaults
parse-constraint-narrows-a-default
parse-constraint-empties-a-disjunct
# A FAILURE TO PARSE IS A FAILURE TO UNIFY here too.
parse-constraint-refuses-text-outside-the-grammar
parse-constraint-refuses-the-empty-string
parse-constraint-refuses-a-grammar-that-does-not-compile
# THE CONSTRAINT HOLDS while it has no value to check: a peer that is
# not a settled string keeps both terms, so the constraint survives to
# meet a value on a later pass and refuses at generation if none comes.
parse-constraint-holds-for-a-non-string
parse-constraint-holds-unmet
parse-constraint-holds-for-an-unsettled-grammar
# A grammar that does not compile is refused at a two-argument call
# too, and not only where it is declared: the call may spell it inline.
parse-refuses-a-grammar-that-does-not-compile
# A NIL PASSES THROUGH every argument position and both forms
# unchanged, so the refusal a reader sees is the one that happened
# rather than a second one about parsing.
abnf-refuses-a-nil-argument
parse-refuses-a-nil-grammar
parse-refuses-a-nil-argument
parse-constraint-refuses-a-nil-peer
# SHAPING THE TREE. The answer is the RAW tree, so a document that wants
# natural structure builds it with the language's own verbs: pick()
# projects one field of every child, filter() selects children by rule,
# and join() folds a one-element selection back to a scalar. These rows
# are the worked examples, and they also pin the two facts about the
# tree's SHAPE that a grammar author has to know.
# One child per field, each keeping its rule name.
shape-projects-every-child
column3:
G: hide(abnf("ver = \"v\" maj \".\" min \".\" pat\nmaj = 1*DIGIT\nmin = 1*DIGIT\npat = 1*DIGIT\nDIGIT = %x30-39\n"))
t: hide(parse($.G, "v1.2.30"))
parts: pick($.t.kids, src)
names: pick($.t.kids, rule)

column1: # A LEADING FIELD LOSES ITS NAME. The converter folds a production's
# first element into the parent's node, so `ver = maj "." min "." pat`
# answers a first child named DIGIT where the row above answers `maj`.
# The fix is the row above: give the production a leading terminal.
# Identical in both ports, so it is a property of the grammar
# compiler and not a parity break.
shape-a-leading-field-loses-its-name
column3:
G: hide(abnf("ver = maj \".\" min \".\" pat\nmaj = 1*DIGIT\nmin = 1*DIGIT\npat = 1*DIGIT\nDIGIT = %x30-39\n"))
t: hide(parse($.G, "1.2.30"))
parts: pick($.t.kids, src)
names: pick($.t.kids, rule)

column1: # filter() by rule is how a field is read out by name; join() over a
# one-element projection is how it comes back as a scalar rather than a
# list. The whole match is always `src` on the root node.
shape-selects-one-field-by-rule
column3:
G: hide(abnf("media = \"@\" type \"/\" sub\ntype = 1*ALPHA\nsub = 1*ALPHA\nALPHA = %x61-7A\n"))
t: hide(parse($.G, "@text/plain"))
type: join(pick(filter($.t.kids, {rule:"type"}), src))
sub: join(pick(filter($.t.kids, {rule:"sub"}), src))
whole: $.t.src

column1: # A repetition answers one child per iteration.
shape-a-repetition-is-one-child-each
column3: G: hide(abnf("dur = \\"P\\" seg *seg\\nseg = num unit\\nnum = 1*DIGIT\\nunit = \\"h\\" / \\"m\\" / \\"s\\"\\nDIGIT = %x30-39\\n"))\nt: hide(parse($.G, "P1h30m45s"))\nsegs: pick($.t.kids, src)

column1: # The classic dotted quad, four children of one rule.
shape-a-dotted-quad
column3: G: hide(abnf("ip = \\"#\\" o \\".\\" o \\".\\" o \\".\\" o\\no = 1*3DIGIT\\nDIGIT = %x30-39\\n"))\nt: hide(parse($.G, "#192.168.0.1"))\noctets: pick($.t.kids, src)
